questions.question: By what does Allah swear in the opening verse of Surah Al-Balad?
options: By the Prophet's lineage
By the city of Mecca
By the night and the day
By the heavens and the earth
questions.explanation: The verse 'la uqsimu bi-hadha al-balad' is a divine oath sworn by the city of Mecca. Imam al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir both affirm that this oath honors Mecca as the most sacred place on earth, the site of the Kaaba and the birthplace of the Prophet Muhammad.

questions.question: True or false: The word 'kabad' in verse 4 indicates that human beings were created in a state of ease and effortless existence.
questions.explanation: The opposite is true. 'Kabad' means hardship, toil, and intense struggle. Ibn Abbas explained that man was created 'in hardship,' and Said ibn Jubayr added that this includes 'the struggle for livelihood,' indicating that hardship is the very environment in which human life unfolds.

questions.question: What does the boastful man in verse 6 claim, saying 'ahlaktu malan lubada'?
options: I have given charity in secret
I have built a great house
I have spent wealth in abundance
I have freed many slaves
questions.explanation: The phrase means 'I have spent wealth in abundance,' a boast of lavish expenditure. Ibn Kathir notes that the verb 'ahlaktu' literally means 'I have destroyed,' revealing that the spending was reckless and self-serving rather than a sincere act of charity for Allah's sake.

questions.question: What does 'al-najdayn' (the two ways) in verse 10 most commonly refer to according to the majority of classical commentators?
options: The two paths of Mecca and Medina
The paths of good and evil
The two paths of trade and pilgrimage
The paths of the rich and the poor
questions.explanation: Ibn Kathir records that Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and many companions and successors understood al-najdayn as the two paths of good and evil. The word 'najd' refers to an elevated, conspicuous road, indicating that both moral paths are clearly visible to anyone who reflects.

questions.question: True or false: According to Imam al-Qurtubi, the protection of sight is one of the necessities (daruriyyat) safeguarded by Islamic law.
questions.explanation: Al-Qurtubi notes that the preservation of sight is among the five necessities protected by Islamic law (daruriyyat al-shari'ah), alongside life, intellect, lineage, and property. By foregrounding the gift of two eyes, the verse reminds the arrogant person that his very capacity to function was given as a divine gift.

questions.question: Which hadith does Ibn Kathir cite in connection with verse 13 about freeing a slave (fakku raqabah)?
options: A hadith stating that prayer is the pillar of religion
The hadith from Abu Hurayra that whoever frees a Muslim slave, Allah will save his every limb from the Fire in proportion to the limbs of the one freed
A hadith forbidding business at the time of the Friday call to prayer
A hadith establishing the obligation of Hajj once in a lifetime
questions.explanation: Ibn Kathir cites the hadith from Abu Hurayra recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim that whoever frees a believing slave will be saved from the Fire limb for limb. Imam al-Qurtubi further connects this verse to manumission as a kaffarah (expiation) in Islamic law.

questions.question: True or false: According to the hadith cited by Imam al-Qurtubi, giving sadaqah to a relative carries a double reward — the reward of charity and the reward of maintaining family ties.
questions.explanation: Imam al-Qurtubi cites the hadith in Sahih Muslim in which the Prophet stated that giving sadaqah to a relative carries a double reward: the reward of sadaqah and the reward of silat al-rahim. This is why feeding 'an orphan of near kinship' (yatiman dha maqrabah) is especially meritorious.

questions.question: According to Wahbah al-Zuhayli in al-Tafsir al-Munir, why is the reward for the companions of the right (ashab al-maymana) announced so briefly in verse 18?
options: Because the reward is uncertain and conditional on further deeds
Because the surah was revealed in haste
Because divine reward is stated concisely once it is unconditionally earned, mirroring its definitive nature
Because the reward applies only to the Prophet's family
questions.explanation: Wahbah al-Zuhayli observes that after the long description of the aqabah's difficulty, the reward is announced with swift certainty. This brevity reflects the Quranic principle that divine reward may be stated concisely because it is unconditional and definitive once earned through righteous striving.

questions.question: True or false: Sayyid Qutb in Fi Zilal al-Quran reads verse 17 as defining the believing community as one held together by mutual moral covenant of patience and mercy, rather than by blood, tribe, or interest.
questions.explanation: Sayyid Qutb offers an influential reading that verse 17 defines the 'organic' quality of the believing community (jama'a): it is held together not by blood, tribe, or worldly interest, but by mutual moral covenant — the wills of its members aligned toward sabr (patience) and marhamah (compassion).
